Mini-Lesson

Christianity: Significant social and historical developments in religious thought (part 1)

5 missions. Guess, learn, then check. Your place is saved.

  1. Mission 1Jesus warned that riches make it hard to reach God's Kingdom. Why do some churches say God wants you rich?
  2. Mission 2Britain is now a land of many faiths. How should Christians live with neighbours who believe differently?
  3. Mission 3Missionaries once sailed from Britain to the world. Why do some now come to Britain to do the same?
  4. Mission 4Christians believe Jesus came to save all people. But Jesus was a man: can a male saviour save women?
  5. Mission 5Some feminists stayed in the Church to change it. Why did others decide they had to leave?
Mission 1

Mission 1: Jesus warned that riches make it hard to reach God's Kingdom. Why do some churches say God wants you rich?

Make a guess: Jesus warned that riches make it hard to reach God's Kingdom. Why do some churches say God wants you rich?

Mission 1

Materialism: the secular challenge

  • Materialism (here): treating money and possessions as the main source of happiness, success and meaning.
  • Consumerism: a culture in which buying and owning things shapes identity.
  • In a secular society, wealth can replace God as the goal of life: you are what you earn and own.
  • Christians respond in very different ways: warning against wealth, using it as a trust, renouncing it, or (some) treating it as God's reward.
Mission 1Read the source

The rich man (Mark 10:17–25)

A rich man asks Jesus how to inherit eternal life. He has kept the commandments.

> "One thing you lack. Go, sell whatever you have and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me, taking up the cross." (Mark 10:21, WEBBE)

> "It is easier for a camel to go through a needle's eye than for a rich man to enter into God's Kingdom." (Mark 10:25, WEBBE)

  • The man "went away sorrowful, for he was one who had great possessions" (Mark 10:22).

Q1 What stopped the man following Jesus?

Show answer

His attachment to his possessions.

Q2 Is the command in verse 21 given to everyone, or to this man?

Show answer

Christians disagree: most read it as addressed to him; some, such as early monks, took it as a call for themselves.

Mission 1

The dangers of wealth

  • Divided loyalty: "You can't serve both God and Mammon" (Matthew 6:24). Mammon: wealth treated as a master.
  • Anxiety: Jesus tells followers not to be anxious about food or clothes, but to "seek first God's Kingdom and his righteousness" (Matthew 6:33; whole passage 6:25–34).
  • The heart follows the treasure: "where your treasure is, there will your heart be also" (Luke 12:34; see 12:33).
  • Love of money: "For the love of money is a root of all kinds of evil." (1 Timothy 6:10)
  • The target is trust in and love of wealth, not money as such.
  • These four passages are your set references for the dangers of wealth.
Quick check
?According to 1 Timothy 6:10, where does the danger of wealth lie?
Mission 1

Stewardship: wealth as a trust

  • Stewardship: everything belongs to God; humans manage it on God's behalf. "The earth is the LORD's, with its fullness" (Psalm 24:1).
  • Humans are placed in the garden "to cultivate and keep it" (Genesis 2:15).
  • The Parable of the Talents (Matthew 25:14–30): servants are praised for using what they are given well.
  • The rich are told "to do good, … to be rich in good works, … ready to distribute, willing to share" (1 Timothy 6:18; see 6:17).
  • John Wesley (1703–1791), sermon "The Use of Money" (1760): "Gain all you can", "save all you can", "give all you can".
  • On this view wealth is good if it is gained honestly and used for God and neighbour.
Mission 1

The ascetic ideal

  • Asceticism: giving up comforts and possessions to grow closer to God.
  • Antony of Egypt (c. 251–356) heard Jesus' words "go, sell what you have, and give to the poor" (Matthew 19:21), gave away his land and lived in the desert (Athanasius, Life of Antony, c. 360).
  • Monastic vows: Benedictine monks and nuns hold all things in common (Rule of St Benedict, c. 530); Francis of Assisi (1181/2–1226) embraced radical poverty.
  • The first Christians "had all things in common" (Acts 2:44).
  • Today: religious orders take a vow of poverty; many lay Christians practise simplicity, fasting and generous giving.
Mission 1Diversity

An apparent contradiction?

  • The tension: stewardship says use wealth well; the ascetic ideal says give it up. Both claim Jesus.
  • Clement of Alexandria (c. 150–c. 215), Who Is the Rich Man That Shall Be Saved? (c. 200): Jesus asks the rich man to strip his soul of attachment; wealth used rightly is a tool.
  • Thomas Aquinas (c. 1225–1274) distinguishes commandments (for all) from counsels (poverty, chastity, obedience: for those called to them). A person "can, while using the things of this world, attain to eternal happiness, provided he does not place his end in them" (Summa Theologica I-II q.108 a.4).
  • Martin Luther (1483–1546), On Monastic Vows (1521): rejected a higher spiritual class; every honest calling serves God.
  • So many Christians see two callings, not a contradiction; critics reply that Jesus' words in Mark 10 apply to everyone.
Quick check
?How does Aquinas' distinction between commandments and counsels remove the apparent contradiction between stewardship and asceticism?
Mission 1

The prosperity gospel

  • Taught by the Word-Faith movement, mainly within Pentecostal and charismatic Christianity, strong in the USA, Africa, Latin America and Asia.
  • Roots: E. W. Kenyon (1867–1948); popularised by Kenneth Hagin (1917–2003), Oral Roberts (1918–2009; "seed-faith") and Kenneth Copeland (b. 1936).
  • Health and wealth are God's will for every believer; Jesus' death won both.
  • Positive confession: faith spoken aloud brings what is spoken (critics: "name it and claim it").
  • Seed-faith giving: give to God (often to the ministry), and expect a larger return.
  • Proof texts include 3 John 2, Deuteronomy 8:18, Malachi 3:10, John 10:10 and 2 Corinthians 8:9.
Mission 1Read the source

How the proof texts are read

> "Beloved, I pray that you may prosper in all things and be healthy, even as your soul prospers." (3 John 2, WEBBE)

> "though he was rich, yet for your sakes he became poor, that you through his poverty might become rich." (2 Corinthians 8:9, WEBBE)

  • Word-Faith reading: God wills material prosperity and health; Christ's poverty bought our riches.
  • Critics' reading: 3 John 2 is a standard letter greeting, not a promise. In 2 Corinthians 8–9, Paul is asking a church to give to poor believers in Jerusalem; "rich" means rich in grace.

Q1 What does the critics' reading take into account?

Show answer

The purpose of each letter: a greeting in 3 John; a collection for the poor in 2 Corinthians.

Q2 Why might the Word-Faith reading appeal to people in poverty?

Show answer

It promises God cares about their material needs now, not only after death.

Mission 1Evaluate

Is wealth a sign of God's blessing?

  • Claim: Wealth is a sign of God's blessing on the faithful.
  • For: God blesses Abraham and Job with wealth; God gives "power to get wealth" (Deuteronomy 8:18).
  • For: Supporters say the teaching gives hope, dignity and discipline (hard work, no gambling or drink) to poor communities.
  • Against: Jesus was poor, and blessed the poor (Luke 6:20); Paul knew hunger (Philippians 4:12).
  • Against: It blames the sick and poor for weak faith, and can enrich leaders at their expense. Many churches reject it, e.g. the evangelical Lausanne Movement's Cape Town Commitment (2010).
  • Judgement criteria: Does it read texts in context? Does it fit the cross and suffering? What does it do to the poor?
  • Spec issues: "The extent to which wealth is a sign of God's blessing"; "Whether the ascetic ideal is compatible with Christianity".
Mission 1

Christian responses to materialism today

  • Simplicity: Quakers' testimony to simplicity; Lent fasting; "enough" lifestyles.
  • Generosity: tithing (a tenth of income); giving to charities such as Christian Aid and CAFOD.
  • Justice: Fairtrade; the Jubilee 2000 campaign to cancel the debts of poor countries.
  • Catholic teaching: Pope Francis, Laudato Si' (2015), criticises "compulsive consumerism" and urges a simpler, less wasteful life (§203).
Quick check
?A preacher tells her congregation that God wants every believer to be healthy and rich, and that giving to her ministry will bring back far more. Which movement does this teaching belong to?
Mission check

?A pastor in a poor district tells his church: "Give a seed offering and God will return it a hundredfold. If you stay poor, your faith is weak." A church member replies from the stewardship tradition. Which reply fits that tradition?

Christians agree that wealth is dangerous when it becomes a master; they disagree about whether to use it, give it up, or expect it. A later mission: liberation theology and the poor.

Mission 2

Mission 2: Britain is now a land of many faiths. How should Christians live with neighbours who believe differently?

Make a guess: Britain is now a land of many faiths. How should Christians live with neighbours who believe differently?

Mission 2

How Britain became multi-faith

  • 1948 on: Caribbean migrants (the Windrush generation), mostly Christian.
  • 1950s–70s: migrants from India, Pakistan and Bangladesh bring Islam, Sikhism and Hinduism to British cities.
  • 1968–72: East African Asians arrive from Kenya and Uganda.
  • 1980s on: growing migration from West Africa (Nigeria, Ghana); later from the EU (2004: e.g. Polish Catholics) and as refugees.
  • 2021 Census (England and Wales): Christian 46.2%; no religion 37.2%; Muslim 6.5%; Hindu, Sikh, Buddhist and Jewish communities each 2% or less.
  • Migration has made Britain more religiously diverse and brought many Christians: much church growth in London is in migrant-led churches.
Mission 2

Freedom of religion in a secular state

  • European Convention on Human Rights (1950), Article 9: freedom of thought, conscience and religion, including freedom to change religion and to manifest it "in worship, teaching, practice and observance".
  • Holding a belief is protected absolutely; manifesting it may be limited, but only where limits are lawful and "necessary in a democratic society" (e.g. public safety, others' rights), and no wider than needed (proportionate).
  • In UK law through the Human Rights Act 1998; the Equality Act 2010 makes "religion or belief" a protected characteristic.
  • Secular state: the state does not take sides between religions. Religious pluralism, many faiths with equal rights, is a feature of such states.
  • Britain is a mixed case: an established Church of England, with bishops in the House of Lords, in a pluralist society.
Mission 2

When Christians migrate

  • Many Windrush-era Christians, Anglicans, Methodists and Baptists at home, found a cool welcome in some English churches; many founded their own (e.g. the New Testament Church of God, in Britain from 1953).
  • Assimilation: join existing British churches, or keep a distinct identity?
  • Provision of worship: new congregations rent school halls, buy warehouses or former cinemas; planning permission and noise can be issues.
  • Style of worship: often lively, Pentecostal or Charismatic; long services; prayer and preaching in the home language.
  • Culture: second and third generations may prefer English-language worship; tension between keeping heritage and reaching British neighbours.
  • Other migrant churches: Polish Catholic parishes; Romanian and Eritrean Orthodox communities; Chinese and Korean churches.
Mission 2

Evangelical and Pentecostal growth

  • Evangelicals stress conversion, the Bible, the cross and active mission (David Bebbington's four marks, 1989).
  • Pentecostalism: from the Azusa Street revival, Los Angeles, 1906 (led by William J. Seymour); baptism in the Holy Spirit, speaking in tongues, healing, as in Acts 2.
  • Charismatic renewal (from the 1960s): the same gifts in Catholic, Anglican and other mainline churches.
  • Rapid growth in Africa, Latin America and Asia: the centre of gravity of Christianity has moved to the global South.
Mission 2

The African diaspora and reverse mission

  • African-led churches in Britain include the Redeemed Christian Church of God (founded in Nigeria, 1952), Kingsway International Christian Centre (London, 1992) and Aladura churches (e.g. Cherubim and Seraphim).
  • Features: strong prayer life, healing, prosperity teaching in some, community support for new migrants.
  • Reverse mission: Christians from countries once evangelised by Britain now send missionaries to Britain, which they see as needing re-evangelising after secularisation.
  • E.g. the RCCG aims to plant churches within a few minutes' walk of people in every country.
  • Questions: most members are migrants; reaching white British neighbours is harder. Supporters reply that growth is real and that the second generation is bridging the gap.
Quick check
?What does "reverse mission" mean?
Mission 2Evaluate

Should Christians try to convert people of other faiths?

  • Claim: Christians in a multi-faith society should seek to convert people of other faiths.
  • For: The Great Commission: "make disciples of all nations" (Matthew 28:19); exclusivist reading of John 14:6.
  • For: Reverse mission shows the energy of churches that still see evangelism as central.
  • Against: Pluralists: other faiths are valid paths; conversion is unnecessary and may harm community relations.
  • Against: Pressure to convert can damage trust between communities; community support and service to neighbours may witness better.
  • Judgement criteria: What do Christians believe about salvation? Can mission be respectful? Does it serve social cohesion? Does freedom of religion include the freedom to persuade?
  • Most UK churches, migrant-led ones included, combine witness with dialogue and practical co-operation with neighbours of other faiths.
Mission check

?A town council plans to ban door-to-door visits by all religious groups, because some residents feel pressured. Under Article 9 of the European Convention on Human Rights, which principle is at stake?

Freedom of religion covers sharing faith as well as holding it. Living with neighbours means balancing that freedom with theirs.

Mission 3

Mission 3: Missionaries once sailed from Britain to the world. Why do some now come to Britain to do the same?

Make a guess: Missionaries once sailed from Britain to the world. Why do some now come to Britain to do the same?

Mission 3

What Christians mean by mission

  • Mission (Latin mittere, to send): the Church's task of being sent into the world.
  • Evangelism: one part of mission: sharing the gospel ("good news") of Jesus so that people may come to faith.
  • Many Christians also count service (care, healing, education), justice and dialogue as mission.
  • Debates in this mission: Is mission mainly about converting people? Who sends whom? How should Christians share faith among people of other religions and none?
Mission 3Read the source

The Great Commission

> "Go and make disciples of all nations, baptising them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to observe all things that I commanded you." (Matthew 28:19–20, WEBBE)

> "You will be witnesses to me in Jerusalem, in all Judea and Samaria, and to the uttermost parts of the earth." (Acts 1:8, WEBBE)

  • Christians take these words of the risen Jesus as the mandate for mission.

Q1 Which three activities does Matthew 28:19–20 name?

Show answer

Making disciples, baptising, teaching.

Q2 Why might Acts 1:8 suggest that mission spreads outward from a centre?

Show answer

It moves from Jerusalem, to the surrounding regions, to the ends of the earth.

Mission 3

How ideas of mission changed

  • 1910, Edinburgh: mission pictured as going from the "Christian West" to the "non-Christian world".
  • 1952, Willingen: mission is missio Dei, God's own mission; the Church does not own mission but takes part in what God is already doing.
  • 1963, Mexico City: "mission in six continents": every continent, the West included, is a mission field.
  • 1965, Vatican II, Ad Gentes: the whole Church is missionary by its nature. 1975, Evangelii Nuntiandi (Paul VI): evangelisation includes witness of life and changing society.
  • 1974, Lausanne Congress (evangelicals; John Stott, Billy Graham): evangelism and social action are both Christian duty.
  • 1984–90, Anglican Five Marks of Mission: tell, teach, tend, transform, treasure creation.
  • Shift in short: from sending to "heathen lands" to mission from everywhere to everywhere, with word and deed.
Mission 3

Reverse mission

  • By the late 20th century most Christians lived in the global South (Africa, Asia, Latin America). Andrew Walls (1928–2021) and Philip Jenkins (The Next Christendom, 2002) traced this shift.
  • Reverse mission: Christians from former mission fields come to evangelise Europe and Britain, which they see as having drifted from faith.
  • Examples: the Redeemed Christian Church of God (founded in Nigeria, 1952; UK parishes since the late 1980s); Kingsway International Christian Centre (London, 1992); Latin American and Korean churches; Polish Catholic priests serving migrants.
  • Forerunner: Lesslie Newbigin (1909–1998), back from nearly forty years in India, argued that Western culture itself is a mission field (Foolishness to the Greeks, 1986).
  • Debate: research suggests many such churches mostly reach people of their own diaspora; leaders and scholars disagree about how far they reach white British people.
Mission 3

Evangelism in a pluralist, secular age

  • Pluralism: many faiths side by side; claims that one faith is uniquely true can seem arrogant. Secularisation: religion has less public weight.
  • Newbigin: in a pluralist society Christians should offer the gospel as public truth, humbly, not as private opinion.
  • Methods: courses such as Alpha (from Holy Trinity Brompton, London; widely used since the 1990s); Fresh Expressions of church; social action (foodbanks, street pastors); online and social media witness.
  • Objections: evangelism may disrespect other faiths or exploit vulnerable people; secular critics, and some Christians, prefer presence and service.
  • Replies: freedom of religion includes freedom to share and change belief; Christians are told to give a reason for their hope "with humility and fear" (1 Peter 3:15).
Quick check
?Which description best fits the reverse mission movement?
Mission 3Evaluate

Is mission still relevant to the spread of Christianity?

  • Claim: Mission and evangelism are no longer appropriate in a pluralist, secular society.
  • For: Many people see seeking converts as disrespectful of other faiths and of non-belief.
  • For: The link between historic mission and colonialism damaged trust.
  • Against: Christianity grew worldwide in the 20th century largely through local evangelism; mission still spreads belief.
  • Against: Mission has broadened: service, justice and dialogue sit beside proclamation (e.g. the Five Marks of Mission).
  • Against: Reverse mission shows that former mission fields still see evangelism as good news to share.
  • Judgement criteria: What counts as mission (conversion only, or word and deed)? Is respect compatible with seeking to persuade? Is the UK a mission field?
  • Issue in your spec: "The extent to which the UK is a modern mission field."
Mission check

?A church in Leeds is led by a pastor from Ghana. It runs a foodbank, holds a weekly course explaining the Christian faith, and joins an iftar meal at a local mosque. A critic says: "That isn't mission. Mission means sending people overseas to convert others." Which reply best reflects how Christian ideas of mission have developed since 1910?

The direction of mission has turned around, and its meaning has widened. Next: how mission at Edinburgh 1910 also started the search for Christian unity.

Mission 4

Mission 4: Christians believe Jesus came to save all people. But Jesus was a man: can a male saviour save women?

Make a guess: Christians believe Jesus came to save all people. But Jesus was a man: can a male saviour save women?

Mission 4

What is feminist theology?

  • Patriarchy: a social system in which men hold power and male experience is treated as the norm.
  • Feminist theology asks how patriarchy has shaped Christian scripture, doctrine, worship and leadership, and what should follow.
  • Context: first-wave feminism (votes for women; Elizabeth Cady Stanton, The Woman's Bible, 1895–98); second-wave feminism of the 1960s–70s.
  • Key themes: women's experience as a source for theology; a hermeneutic of suspicion (reading texts alert to male bias: Elisabeth Schüssler Fiorenza, In Memory of Her, 1983); language for God (McFague).
  • Two paths: reform Christianity from within (Ruether, McFague) or leave it as beyond repair.
Mission 4

Rosemary Radford Ruether

  • Rosemary Radford Ruether (1936–2022), American Catholic theologian; Sexism and God-Talk (1983).
  • Her critical principle: whatever denies or diminishes "the full humanity of women" is not redemptive; whatever promotes it reflects the divine (paraphrase, ch. 1).
  • She is a reformist: she stays within Christianity and recovers its prophetic-liberating tradition, in which God sides with the oppressed.
  • Chapter 5 asks the question of this mission: "Can a Male Saviour Save Women?"
Mission 4

The problem of a male Christ

  • Over centuries, Christ's maleness was used to rank men above women.
  • Aquinas, following Aristotle, wrote that as an individual, "woman is defective and misbegotten" (Summa Theologica I q.92 a.1 ad 1), while insisting that woman is part of God's plan for human nature.
  • Christ's maleness has been used to argue that only men can represent Christ as priests.
  • An early Christian principle: what Christ did not take on, he did not heal (Gregory of Nazianzus, 4th century). If Christ's maleness is what saves, women seem left out.
  • Ruether: Christ's maleness has no ultimate significance; it matters only as a social symbol in patriarchal societies.
Mission 4

Jesus against the warrior-messiah

  • Many Jews of Jesus' time hoped for a Messiah like King David: a warrior who would defeat Israel's enemies and rule.
  • Ruether: Jesus rejected that model of power. He came as a servant, not a ruler:

> "whoever wants to become great amongst you shall be your servant." (Mark 10:43, WEBBE)

  • He sided with the marginalised: the poor, outcasts, women. Women followed him and were first witnesses of the resurrection (Luke 24:9–10).
  • So Jesus' life announces the "kenosis of patriarchy" (Ruether's phrase): the self-emptying of male power.
  • His maleness, read this way, is a critique of patriarchy, not a support for it.
Mission 4Read the source

Wisdom, a female figure

> "Doesn't wisdom cry out? Doesn't understanding raise her voice?" (Proverbs 8:1, WEBBE)

> "For she is a reflection of everlasting light, an unspotted mirror of the working of God, and an image of his goodness." (Wisdom 7:26, WEBBE)

  • In Hebrew, wisdom is hokmah; in Greek, sophia. Both are feminine, and the texts personify Wisdom as a woman who is with God at creation (Proverbs 8:22–31).
  • Ruether: Wisdom is a female principle in God; early Christians called Christ "the wisdom of God" (1 Corinthians 1:24). John's Logos (Word) took over her role.

Q1 What role does Wisdom have in God's work?

Show answer

She reflects God's light and goodness; she is present at creation.

Q2 Why does this matter for the male-saviour question?

Show answer

If Jesus is the incarnation of a female Wisdom, Christ is not simply male.

Quick check
?How does Ruether answer the question "Can a male saviour save women?"
Mission 4

The androgynous Christ and the Christlike female

  • Androgynous Christ: Christ unites "masculine" and "feminine" qualities (e.g. Julian of Norwich, Revelations of Divine Love, c. 1395, calls Jesus "our Mother").
  • Ruether values the aim but warns that many androgynous pictures still treat the male as the norm and the "feminine" as a mere side of him.
  • Her own answer: Christ is not confined to the historical Jesus. The Christian community continues Christ's identity, so Christ can be met "in the form of our sister" (Ruether's phrase).
  • The Christlike female: Jesus came to the last and least. Women, among the most marginalised, can show the liberated humanity Christ brings in a fuller way than men who keep power: the last become first (Matthew 20:16).
Mission 4Diversity

Responses to Ruether

  • Catholic and Orthodox teaching: Christ saves all humans because he took on human nature; maleness is not what saves. But his maleness still matters as a sign, e.g. for priesthood.
  • Many evangelicals: Christ is defined by scripture and the creeds; the historical Jesus cannot be replaced by a community's Christ.
  • Other feminists: Elizabeth Johnson, She Who Is (1992), develops a fuller Sophia (Wisdom) Christology.
  • Daphne Hampson: Ruether picks only the parts she likes; a Christianity tied to a male past cannot be made feminist (see Mission 5).
Quick check
?What is a "hermeneutic of suspicion" in feminist theology?
Mission 4Evaluate

Can a male saviour save women?

  • Claim: A male saviour can save women.
  • For: The creeds stress that Christ became human (incarnation), not male; Galatians 3:28: in Christ "neither male nor female".
  • For: Ruether: Jesus' life overturns patriarchal power.
  • For: Ruether: Christ as Wisdom is not only male.
  • Against: Christ's maleness has been used for centuries to exclude women; symbols shape power (Daly).
  • Against: Hampson: the uniqueness of one historical man makes the male normative for ever.
  • Judgement criteria: What saves: Christ's humanity or his maleness? Can tradition be reinterpreted this far? What effects do the symbols have on real women?
Mission check

?A Christian group rewrites some of its prayers to call God "Wisdom" and "she" alongside "Father". Its members say they are reclaiming forgotten parts of the Bible and want to change the Church, not leave it. Which approach is this closest to?

Reformist feminists such as Ruether read Christ as one who empties patriarchy of its power. Next: Daly and Hampson, who decided Christianity could not be saved.

Mission 5

Mission 5: Some feminists stayed in the Church to change it. Why did others decide they had to leave?

Make a guess: Some feminists stayed in the Church to change it. Why did others decide they had to leave?

Mission 5

Reform or leave?

  • All feminist theologians agree that Christianity has been shaped by patriarchy.
  • Reformists (Ruether, McFague, Johnson): the core of Christianity is liberating; remove the sexism and stay.
  • Post-Christian feminists (Daly, Hampson): the sexism is built in; Christianity cannot be repaired, so they left.
  • Post-Christian does not mean atheist: both kept a spirituality; Hampson still believes in God.
  • The question: is patriarchy a stain on Christianity, or part of its structure?
Mission 5

Mary Daly

  • Mary Daly (1928–2010), American Catholic philosopher and theologian; taught at Boston College (a Jesuit university).
  • The Church and the Second Sex (1968): a reformist call for change.
  • Beyond God the Father (1973): now post-Christian: "if God is male, then the male is God".
  • The male symbol of God sanctions male rule in church, family and society.
  • God is not a noun but a verb: "Be-ing", the power of becoming in which women share.
  • Later: Gyn/Ecology (1978) and Pure Lust (1984).
Mission 5

The "unholy trinity"

  • Beyond God the Father, ch. 4: patriarchy produces a "phallic morality" of domination.
  • Its fruits Daly calls an unholy trinity: rape, genocide and war.
  • She sets it against the Christian Trinity: Father, Son and a Spirit often imagined as male, a sacred image of male power.
  • Her argument (paraphrase): a religion whose highest symbols are male trains societies to accept male violence and to blame women (the scapegoating of Eve).
  • So the problem is not a few sexist verses: it runs through the symbols themselves.
Mission 5

Spirituality through nature

  • Daly calls women to leave patriarchal religion and find a spirituality of "Be-ing".
  • Beyond God the Father, ch. 6: sisterhood as a "cosmic covenant": harmony with all life and the natural world.
  • Gyn/Ecology: patriarchy's domination of women and its domination of nature are linked; liberation of both belongs together (a root of ecofeminism).
  • Spirituality is found in women's experience, community and nature, not in church, creed or male priesthood.
Quick check
?In Daly's argument, what does the "unholy trinity" name?
Mission 5

Daphne Hampson

  • Daphne Hampson (b. 1944), British theologian (St Andrews); Theology and Feminism (1990); After Christianity (1996). Once active in the campaign for women priests.
  • Christianity is "irredeemably sexist" because it is a historical religion: it claims a unique revelation of God in a particular past.
  • That past was patriarchal: a male Jesus, God as Father and Son, male apostles. Christians must always look back to it, so the bias can never be removed.
  • Not moral: feminism needs full equality now. Not true: after the Enlightenment, she argues, a unique divine act in one time and place is not credible.
  • She is a post-Christian theist: she believes in God, known through human experience, but not in Christ's uniqueness.
Mission 5Read the source

"Neither male nor female"

> "There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither slave nor free man, there is neither male nor female; for you are all one in Christ Jesus." (Galatians 3:28, WEBBE)

  • Reformists (Ruether): this is the liberating core of the Gospel; later sexism betrays it.
  • Hampson: one verse, written by a man in a patriarchal world, cannot outweigh the structure of a religion centred on a male saviour and a Father God.

Q1 How would Ruether use this verse?

Show answer

As evidence that equality is part of Christianity's original message.

Q2 Why does Hampson think it is not enough?

Show answer

Christianity remains tied to a male past; the problem is structural, not a matter of verses.

Quick check
?Why does Hampson describe Christianity as irredeemably sexist?
Mission 5Diversity

Ruether, Daly and Hampson compared

  • Is Christianity patriarchal? All three: yes, deeply.
  • Can it be reformed? Ruether: yes, from its prophetic core. Daly and Hampson: no.
  • What about Jesus? Ruether: he empties male power. Daly: Christ-worship sanctifies maleness. Hampson: his uniqueness makes the male normative.
  • God? Ruether: God/ess, the primal Matrix (her terms). Daly: God as Verb, Be-ing. Hampson: God known in experience, beyond any tradition.
  • Where do they go? Ruether stays in the Catholic Church and helps shape the Women-Church movement. Daly and Hampson leave.
Mission 5Evaluate

Can Christianity be changed, or should it be abandoned?

  • Claim: Christianity is essentially sexist and should be abandoned.
  • For: Hampson: a historical religion is tied to a patriarchal past; Daly: Christ-worship sanctifies maleness.
  • For: Centuries of reform have left many churches still male-led.
  • Against: Ruether: the prophetic tradition and Jesus' practice contain the critique of patriarchy; Galatians 3:28.
  • Against: Real change has happened: women priests and bishops; inclusive language; female images of God.
  • Against (traditional Christians): God has no sex; equal dignity with different roles is not sexism.
  • Judgement criteria: Is sexism the structure or a distortion? Is a religion defined by its origins or by how it develops? Does reform answer Hampson's point about the past?
Mission 5

Impact on believers and communities

  • Language: inclusive-language Bibles, hymns and liturgies (e.g. "humankind" for "mankind").
  • Ministry: feminist theology fed the case for ordaining women.
  • Communities: Women-Church groups and women's liturgies; feminist biblical scholarship taught in many seminaries.
  • Limits: the Catholic and Orthodox Churches keep an all-male priesthood; many Christians reject feminist theology as shaped by secular ideology.
  • Spec issues: "The extent to which feminist theology impacts modern Christian practice"; "Whether men and women are equal in Christianity".
Mission check

?Priya leaves her church after many years. She still prays and believes in God, but says: "No religion that looks back to one man, in one patriarchal age, as God's unique revelation can ever treat women as equals." Whose position is closest to Priya's?

Reformists and post-Christians agree that Christianity has been patriarchal; they disagree on whether that is a stain or the structure.

Recap

The big ideas

Mission 1

  • Jesus and the New Testament warn against trusting and loving wealth (Mark 10:17–25; Matthew 6:24–34; Luke 12:33–34; 1 Timothy 6:10).
  • Stewardship treats wealth as God's trust to be used well; the ascetic ideal gives it up; the Word-Faith prosperity gospel treats it as God's promised blessing.
  • Aquinas, Clement and Luther show ways of holding stewardship and asceticism together.

Mission 2

  • Migration since 1948 has made Britain multi-faith and brought new Christian communities; Article 9 protects belief and, within limits, its expression.
  • Migrant churches face challenges of assimilation, buildings, worship style and culture; African-led and Pentecostal churches have grown, and some see their work as reverse mission.

Mission 3

  • Mission is the Church being sent (Matthew 28:19–20); evangelism is one part of it.
  • Since 1910 the picture changed: from West-to-rest conversion to missio Dei and mission from everywhere to everywhere, in word and deed; reverse mission sends Christians from the global South to Britain.

Mission 4

  • Feminist theology examines patriarchy in Christianity; reformists stay to change it, post-Christians leave.
  • Ruether (Sexism and God-Talk, 1983): Jesus rejected the warrior-messiah; his maleness has no ultimate significance; Christ can be met in women.
  • Ruether: Christ is Wisdom (Sophia), a female figure in the Bible.

Mission 5

  • Daly: worshipping Christ sanctifies maleness, so she left Christianity.
  • Daly (Beyond God the Father, 1973): if God is male, the male is God; God as Be-ing.
  • Daly: patriarchy's unholy trinity of rape, genocide and war; spirituality in harmony with nature.
  • Hampson (Theology and Feminism, 1990): Christianity is irredeemably sexist because it is tied to a unique, patriarchal past; she remains a theist.
  • Ruether reforms from within; Daly and Hampson leave.
